clue.text: Goals reconceived in Nigeria

indicators.note: to reconceive is to form afresh, so the letters of the word before it are formed into a new order

explanation.surface: A football team's targets get rethought on a trip to Nigeria.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reconceived' rearranges GOALS. The definition is 'in Nigeria': the answer is a city found there.
explanation.definitionFit: Lagos is Nigeria's largest city and former capital.

clue.text: Which labour wings support Militant if not interfered with?

explanation.surface: Asks which wings of the Labour Party back the Militant faction, if nobody meddles.
explanation.walkthrough: Militant (the Militant Tendency) was a hard-left group inside Britain's Labour Party, so of Labour's two wings it backs the left one only. The phrase also means undisturbed.
explanation.definitionFit: Militant supports only the leftward wing of the party; separately, the phrase is an idiom for being undisturbed by others.

clue.text: Loss of his initial gamble would reveal his fatherland

definitions.text: Loss of his initial gamble would reveal his fatherland

parts.words: Loss of his initial gamble would reveal his fatherland
parts.note: an agent from Berlin whose first gamble fails, and who is caught, has his nationality exposed; the clue also hints that dropping the S of the second word leaves letters close to his country's name

explanation.surface: A gambler's first lost bet gives away where he comes from.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as the story of a wartime agent: if his first risky move fails, his true home country is exposed.
explanation.definitionFit: A wartime agent from Berlin who is caught on his first gamble has his homeland made known.

clue.text: One who looks a man of vision

explanation.surface: Someone peering about turns out to be a visionary.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally one who sees, and also a prophet who has visions of the future.

clue.text: Start sketching out how far you are prepared to go?

definitions.text: how far you are prepared to go

explanation.surface: An artist begins a drawing and asks how far they will take it.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally pencil a first stroke; idiomatically set a limit beyond which you will not go.

clue.text: Ran London borough by skulduggery

parts.note: to double is to run at speed, as soldiers move 'at the double', so ran gives doubled
Ealing is a borough in west London

explanation.surface: Someone ran a London council by underhand methods.
explanation.walkthrough: EALING is a borough of west London. 'Ran' looks like 'managed' but gives DOUBLED, as in running at the double.
explanation.definitionFit: Duplicity and trickery, acting one way while secretly doing another, are skulduggery.

clue.text: Swear like a clergyman upset

indicators.note: in a down clue upset turns the word for clergyman upside down, so it reads from the bottom up

parts.note: Rev, short for Reverend, is the title of a clergyman

explanation.surface: Cursing in the manner of a vicar who has been annoyed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns only REV, giving VER after A. 'like' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: To aver is to state solemnly, to affirm as if on oath.

clue.text: Mental images formed by a supporting real image

indicators.note: in a down clue the letter that supports another sits below it, so it comes after

parts.note: an idol is a physical image of a god, a real one rather than a mental one

explanation.surface: Pictures in the mind are formed by an actual picture held up beneath them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'supporting' puts A beneath IDOL in this down light. Idola is the Latin plural of idolum, a word for a mental image or false notion.
explanation.definitionFit: Idola, plural of idolum, are phantoms or false notions in the mind, as in Bacon's idols of the mind.

clue.text: Anything that occurred in the Seventies

indicators.note: in tells us the answer sits inside the letters of the word that follows

explanation.surface: Asks about anything that happened during the 1970s.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points to the answer inside sEVENTies.
explanation.definitionFit: An occurrence or happening of any kind is an event.

clue.text: Cram into amusing play

explanation.surface: Stuffing too much into a comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: In cookery to farce is to stuff, as with forcemeat; it is also a broadly comic stage piece.

clue.text: As far north as one can go and in real difficulties

definitions.text: As far north as one can go

explanation.surface: An Arctic explorer has reached the limit and is in trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: Up the pole is British slang for being in a mess, or mad; literally it describes reaching the North Pole.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally at the North Pole; as British slang it means in a fix.

clue.text: Committee secretary's job occupying only a short time

explanation.surface: Describes the work of the person keeping records at a meeting.
explanation.definitionFit: Writing the record of a meeting is a secretary's task; the phrase also describes lasting only a few moments.

clue.text: Artilleryman and sailor meet head on with a Moslem

indicators.note: to meet head on, the gunner turns round to face the sailor, so his letters run backwards

parts.note: RA, the Royal Artillery, stands for a gunner
AB, able-bodied seaman, is a sailor

explanation.surface: A gunner and a seaman come face to face with a Muslim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'meet head on' turns RA round to AR, facing AB.
explanation.definitionFit: Most Arabs are Muslims, so the clue's believer stands for an Arab by example.

clue.text: Satisfy one's thirst by finding large pond to the South

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for south
a lake is a large pond

explanation.surface: Quenching your thirst by coming across a southern lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' is a link here: S and LAKE are simply joined.
explanation.definitionFit: To slake is to quench or relieve a thirst.

clue.text: Tempt a university type by sex appeal

parts.note: a BA, Bachelor of Arts, is a university graduate
it is old slang for sex appeal, as in the 'It girl'

explanation.surface: Seducing a student with sheer charm.
explanation.walkthrough: IT for sex appeal comes from the 1927 film 'It' starring Clara Bow.
explanation.definitionFit: Bait is to lure or entice with something attractive.

clue.text: Local game which could turn into an expensive fiddle

definitions.text: which could turn into an expensive fiddle

explanation.surface: A pub game that might become a costly violin.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'local' is a British neighbourhood pub, where darts is played. Rearranged, its letters make STRAD, short for a Stradivarius violin.
explanation.definitionFit: Throwing arrows at a board is a classic pub game, and its letters rearranged spell the short name of a Stradivarius violin.

clue.text: Atkins bar

explanation.surface: Mr Atkins goes to the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: Tommy Atkins is the traditional name for a British private soldier; a tommy bar is a short rod used to turn a box spanner.
explanation.definitionFit: The nickname of the generic British soldier Tommy Atkins, and a tool rod called by the same name.

clue.text: Get on your feet as a way of paying regular bills

definitions.text: a way of paying regular bills

explanation.surface: Rise up, as a way of settling regular bills.
explanation.walkthrough: A standing order is a British bank instruction to pay a fixed sum regularly; read literally, it is a command to stand up.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally a command to rise; in banking, an instruction to pay a fixed sum at regular intervals.

clue.text: Ironic remarks at the expense of the Tory wets?

definitions.text: at the expense of the Tory wets

explanation.surface: Sarcastic jokes aimed at moderate Conservatives.
explanation.walkthrough: In 1980s British politics Thatcher's hardliners were the 'dries' and moderate Tories the 'wets', so the dries' wit would mock the wets.
explanation.definitionFit: Deadpan wit is a deadpan understated humour; and it is the wit of the Thatcherite 'dries' aimed at moderates.

clue.text: Keep at the punch when there is need for .

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held 'Keep at the punch when there is need for .' is cut short: a word or symbol after 'for' is missing, so the second definition cannot be read.
annotationWithheld.clue: Keep at the punch when there is need for .

clue.text: What Ptolemy Caesar had parentally was a well preserved figure

explanation.surface: The son of Cleopatra and an embalmed body from the pyramids.
explanation.walkthrough: Ptolemy Caesar (Caesarion) was the son of Cleopatra, so his mother was an Egyptian 'mummy', British for mother.
explanation.definitionFit: Cleopatra was Ptolemy Caesar's mother, a 'mummy' from Egypt; also an embalmed body from ancient Egypt.

clue.text: Muslin to heat wine

explanation.surface: Using a cloth while warming wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Mull is a fine soft muslin; to mull is also to warm wine with spices.

clue.text: … being prepared to keep dry wine

explanation.surface: Continues the previous clue: getting ready to keep dry with a wine.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as 'mac on', wearing a mackintosh (British for raincoat), it means ready to keep dry; it is also a French Burgundy town and its wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Having a raincoat on keeps you dry; Mâcon is a Burgundy wine region.

clue.text: Joins the golf course

explanation.surface: Signs up at the golf club.
explanation.definitionFit: Links connects things together; it is also a seaside golf course.

clue.text: Foolish fellow makes for a hotel in New York

indicators.note: in puts the lodging word inside the abbreviation for the American city

parts.note: an inn is a small hotel

explanation.surface: A silly man heads for a hotel in Manhattan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'makes for' and 'a' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: A fool or simpleton is a ninny.

clue.text: Unable to say a word in criticism of the stupid blonde

definitions.text: in criticism of the stupid blonde

explanation.surface: Lost for words when criticising a stereotyped blonde.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dumb blonde' is the stock insult the second definition points to.
explanation.definitionFit: Speechless or mute; also the stupid of the stock insult about blondes.

clue.text: Fish wife who outlived Henry

explanation.surface: A fishwife who survived Henry.
explanation.walkthrough: Catherine Parr was the sixth wife of Henry VIII and survived him; a parr is a young salmon.
explanation.definitionFit: A young salmon, and Catherine, the last of Henry VIII's six queens.

clue.text: In the kitchen it turns around and tips up

definitions.text: In the kitchen it turns around

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word is read from the bottom upwards, so the letters run backwards

explanation.surface: Something in the kitchen spins round and then tips over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reverses TIPS in this down light. The definition is a roasting rod that rotates over the fire.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotating rod on which meat is roasted turns round and round in a kitchen.

clue.text: Swindle comes to nothing in old Western Ireland

explanation.surface: A fraud comes to nothing in the west of Ireland long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comes to' and 'in' are link words. The province is now usually spelt Connacht.
explanation.definitionFit: The old spelling of Connacht, the western province of the Irish Republic.

clue.text: Terrorist teacher of course gets nothing after five

indicators.note: after places the letter for nothing behind the Roman five

parts.note: a golf pro teaches players on the course
V is the Roman numeral for five
O, the round figure zero, is nothing

explanation.surface: A gunman who once taught gets nothing after five.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' looks like 'naturally' but means a golf course, whose resident pro teaches. A Provo was a member of the Provisional IRA.
explanation.definitionFit: Provo is short for a member of the Provisional IRA, an armed paramilitary group.

clue.text: Like a wind ensemble given a free hand

explanation.surface: Wind players allowed to do as they please.
explanation.walkthrough: A wind band has no violins, cellos and so on; 'no strings attached' means with no conditions.
explanation.definitionFit: A wind band lacks violins and cellos; the phrase is also an idiom for having no conditions imposed.

clue.text: Doughnut-shaped hill confronts us

definitions.note: the definition is adjectival but names a ring-shaped solid, a noun

parts.note: a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: A ring-shaped hill stands in front of us.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confronts' is a link here: TOR simply comes before US.
explanation.definitionFit: A ring-shaped solid like a bagel is the geometric figure the answer names.
